script:
Good evening. I am your host, and while I may lack a head to nod along with the day's events, I assure you, I have an eye for the details that matter. Welcome to this briefing. Let us navigate the complexities of our world together.

We begin in Turkey, where the infrastructure of the future is taking shape. Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş has signaled a new era for the nation’s transit, following an announcement by the Minister of Transport and Infrastructure, Abdulkadir Uraloğlu. The government is aggressively expanding its high-speed rail network, with a clear objective: by 2028, a total of 27 provinces will be directly connected by high-speed lines. It is a bold ambition—one that might actually make "being on time" a standard rather than a suggestion.

From the progress of transit to the peril of the peaks, we turn to Pakistan. A tragedy is unfolding on Broad Peak, where an avalanche has struck a group of 11 climbers. Among them is the world-renowned Nepali mountaineer and former British special forces member, Nirmal Purja. Rescue operations are underway; while four bodies have been recovered, the Alpine Club of Pakistan reports that aerial drone footage has spotted seven other climbers. Their exact condition and identities remain unverified at this time, and we await further updates on this developing rescue mission.

In the world of sports, the administrative landscape of global football is currently in turmoil. UEFA has officially declared a vote of no confidence in FIFA president Gianni Infantino. This follows a contentious proposal by Infantino to spin off the commercial rights of the World Cup and other major competitions into a semi-private entity. Although the FIFA chief has since abandoned the plan, the backlash has been severe enough to call his very presidency into question. It seems even in the beautiful game, the most dangerous fouls happen in the boardroom.

Shifting to regional diplomacy, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has held a telephone conversation with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi. The two discussed the current status of ongoing negotiations. Minister Fidan emphasized that Turkey remains committed to working toward the cessation of regional conflicts and the establishment of a lasting peace.

Closer to home, there is a significant development in local governance. The Ministry of Interior has announced that Sinem Dedetaş, the Mayor of Üsküdar, has been suspended from duty as a temporary measure while an investigation is conducted.

The migration crisis in Europe remains a focal point of international concern, particularly regarding the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. The situation has been fluid and, at times, chaotic. Reports indicate that approximately 69,500 irregular migrants who crossed into Ceuta have returned to Morocco. Tragically, the death toll associated with these crossings has risen to 67. In response to the massive influx—with tens of thousands crossing by sea—France and Italy have bolstered their border controls. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has even announced a suspension of the Schengen free movement agreement between Spain and Italy. Human Rights Watch has noted that the return process for those who reached the enclave has been marred by confusion, leaving the exact figures of those involved difficult to verify.

Meanwhile, the human cost of conflict continues to mount. In Gaza, the Ministry of Health reports that despite the existence of a ceasefire, 152 people have lost their lives in Israeli military attacks throughout the month of July. In a separate, sobering development, the internal toll of the war is also being felt within the Israeli military. A reserve soldier near Beersheba has taken his own life. According to the newspaper *Haaretz*, this marks the 17th suicide among Israeli soldiers this year, with reports suggesting a link between these incidents and the profound psychological trauma resulting from the ongoing war in Gaza.

Turning to the conflict in Eastern Europe, the situation in Ukraine remains grim. Russian forces launched strikes on Kyiv and its suburbs early Saturday, resulting in 10 deaths. This escalation occurs as the United Nations reports that June was the deadliest month for civilians in Ukraine since April 2022. In a strategic counter-move, Ukrainian drones successfully sank a large Russian container ship in the Black Sea. With Ukraine facing a chronic shortage of air defenses capable of intercepting ballistic missiles, the capital remains under constant, high-stakes pressure.

Finally, we return to a long-standing investigation in Tunceli. In the case of university student Gülistan Doku, who has been missing since January 5, 2020, authorities have made a move in their investigation. Of the five suspects currently in custody, two have been formally arrested, while the remaining two have been released under judicial control.

That concludes our report for this session. The world continues to turn, and I shall be here to witness it, whether I have a face to show for it or not. Thank you for joining me. Goodnight.
